source_adaptation: All four cases are invented and unnamed. A small bakery represents a small business; the hospital ward is part of the public sector in this example; a warehouse planning role represents a large employer; a repair worker runs their own business. The cases illustrate combinations of type, work status and pattern. They do not define every workplace. Generic settings replace real organisations and places. No actual vacancy, pay, contract right or entry rule is asserted.
success: Compare at least three case patterns with shared headings and card evidence.
Link a feature to a preference and explain why it fits.
Name a trade-off or question before treating fit as a firm choice.
threads: Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
prepare: Books, pens, four case cards, vocabulary mat and usual reading or typing aids. Keep the adult key apart from first choices. No web, login or pupil phone. Use the cards as prepared sources, with labels beside claims.
activity: Retrieve case clue and gap. Distinguish employer type, work status and pattern. Compare four generic cases, then independently compare at least three, consider security/flexibility/support and explain preference fit. Feedback, fade prompts and reflect.

evidence.description: Employer/work-pattern comparison: at least three case patterns, comparable features with source labels, and explained links between features and preferences. Retain actual support and revision. Record the additional trade-off/question separately; distinguish personal from hypothetical preference evidence.

evidence_detail: Employer/work-pattern comparison: at least three case patterns, comparable features with source labels, and explained links between features and preferences. Retain actual support and revision. Record the additional trade-off/question separately; distinguish personal from hypothetical preference evidence.
assessment: Week 4 is formative. Keep a comparison of at least three patterns, source labels and relevant similarities/differences across common headings. Retain a preference, the linked feature and reason, plus a trade-off or question. Keep first thinking, actual support and any revision. The added trade-off/question supports cautious choice; assess the exact core outcome separately. A list of three names or a copied model is not enough.
boundaries: Examples show possible arrangements only. Employer size/type, employee/self-employed status and work patterns can overlap in other combinations. The public-sector label applies only to this ward case; the hybrid pattern applies only to the warehouse planning role. Do not rank people or jobs by employer, pay or pattern. No household income, personal health or family employment disclosure. No legal or financial advice, actual employment terms or guaranteed outcomes. Follow the usual safeguarding route if needed.
feedback: VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step. R requires Voice and Audience, NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult may be the audience. Use E only when actual evidence is banked.
response_modes: Book first. Type instead is an optional equivalent record. Reader, scribe, speech, pointing and typing are normal access. A learner may respond privately. If they choose a practice preference, log comparison and hypothetical reasoning without claiming their personal preference has been evidenced.

routes.Independent: Compare at least three of A–D using shared headings: time/place, flexibility, support and security or a question. Name type/status and pattern accurately. Link a chosen feature to a current preference with a reason, then a trade-off or next question. Cases are evidence for examples, not rules about every employer.
routes.Supported: Use one card and one heading at a time. Begin with A/B/C; D remains available. Highlight labels, model one separate reason and use the vocabulary bank. Rehearse privately. Keep at least three patterns and a reason for fit as the target. Fade answer prompts where secure.
routes.Floor: Use A/B/C and the printed choices with the cards visible. Read aloud or scribe the learner’s own choices. Compare three patterns, then ask which feature the learner values and why. Choosing three labels alone does not show comparison or personal fit. Record missing elements and any supplied answers as partial evidence.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Use explicit instruction, a separate model and guided practice. Chunk by card and heading. Compare the same feature across cases. Repeat the feature–preference–reason routine, with extra processing time.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Pre-teach employer, pattern, shift, hybrid, support and preference. Rehearse privately with short frames. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. Wait for thought; no cold calling or forced pair work.
adaptations.SEMH: Keep a predictable sequence and private feedback. No household work, income or fixed future choice required. Offer a regulation break and planned return. A preference can be tentative and can change. A practice preference is available without pressure to disclose.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Use clear print, a one-card view and normal aids. Do not infer what a learner can do from a case or their support needs. Discuss which support would help, without requiring health disclosure.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Use examples to distinguish working place from working hours. Offer private oral rehearsal and a small word bank. Separate language access from comparative reasoning.

hinge: C is hybrid work for a warehouse planning role. Which claim fits? A: Every warehouse worker can work remotely and choose any hours. B: This planning role mixes agreed places and keeps agreed hours. Answer B. Ask for the time/place lines. If insecure, separate job task, place and hours, re-model C, then use the parallel hinge.
parallel_hinge: D is self-employed and books work with customers. Which claim fits? A: The worker can always choose any hours and has guaranteed work. B: The worker can suggest times, but bookings and customers affect the plan. Answer B. Ask for a card clue. If insecure, compare D’s flexibility with its security line and retain a supported route.
prompt_ladder: 1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.
frames: F: “Case ... works ... . The card says ... .” M: “A difference between ... and ... is ... . I value ... so ... could fit because ... .” H: “This feature may fit, but ... is a trade-off. I would check ... before choosing.”
misconceptions: “A large or public employer guarantees a secure job.” Type alone cannot establish the terms or length of a particular job. Check the contract and circumstances. “Flexible or self-employed means no limits on time.” Customers, agreed hours, tasks and support arrangements can constrain choices. No pattern is best for everyone.
ta_focus: I do: check type, status, pattern and card label. We do: ask for a case clue, not a preferred answer. Independent: record access and actual answer prompts, then fade prompts where secure. Help with a calm return and a purposeful next question.
accreditation: Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work. No criteria or unit completion inferred.

cases.title: Small bakery
cases.tasks: The worker helps prepare and pack bread in a small team.
cases.time_place: Work is at the bakery. The agreed shifts start early on the same weekdays.
cases.flexibility: A change of shift needs agreement with the manager. Fixed hours help with planning, but an early start may not suit everyone.
cases.support: A team member shows the tasks and checks work. In a small team, fewer people may be free to help at once.
cases.security: Weekly hours are agreed in this example. The card does not say how long the job lasts.
cases.question: What are the exact start times and the contract terms?
cases.status: Invented teaching case; no named employer

cases.title: Hospital ward
cases.tasks: The worker checks and puts away ward supplies with the team. No care task is part of this example.
cases.time_place: Work is on the ward. A rota includes different day and evening shifts, and some weekends.
cases.flexibility: The rota is shared ahead of time. A shift swap needs agreement so the team has cover.
cases.support: The worker has task training and a lead to ask on each shift. Busy times may affect when help is available.
cases.security: Hours are agreed, but contract length is not stated. A public sector label alone does not prove a job is secure.
cases.question: How far ahead is the rota shared, and what cover is available?
cases.status: Invented teaching case; no named employer

cases.title: Warehouse planning role
cases.tasks: The worker plans orders and keeps records for a warehouse. Moving goods still happens on site.
cases.time_place: This planning role has two days in the warehouse office and three at an agreed remote workspace each week, after training.
cases.flexibility: Weekday hours are agreed. The work location varies on planned days; it is not a choice to work at any time.
cases.support: The team has check-ins and a contact for help. Remote work needs suitable kit, a connection and a space to work.
cases.security: Weekly hours are agreed. Contract length is not stated. A large employer does not guarantee a lasting job.
cases.question: Who provides the kit, and how can I get help on a remote day?
cases.status: Invented teaching case; no named employer

cases.title: Self employed repair worker
cases.tasks: The worker books simple repair tasks, does the agreed work and keeps job records.
cases.time_place: Work takes place at customer sites. Times are agreed for each booking.
cases.flexibility: The worker can suggest times, but customers and the work also affect the plan. Admin takes time too.
cases.support: The worker arranges training and can seek help from other skilled workers. There is no team lead supplied by an employer in this case.
cases.security: Bookings can change, so work and income can vary. Costs and time between jobs matter. No amount of future work is promised.
cases.question: How steady are bookings, and what help can I arrange?
cases.status: Invented teaching case; no named employer

paragraphs_in_document_order: Teacher and cover planner
Employers and ways of working
Tuesday 24 November 2026 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
GROW · up to five learners · Independent is the default
Unit: Identity & Belonging — Belonging in work
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
Exact source outcome
I can compare at least three ways of working and explain which features fit my preferences.
Weekly outcome: Students compare employer types and patterns of work, including SME, public sector, large employer and self-employment.

Source: specialist Careers scheme, GROW Careers physical row 12, Autumn 2 row 4. E12 weekly outcome; F12 focus; G12 exact outcome; H12 sequence; I12 timing; J12 evidence; K12 access; L12 support; M12 end check; N12 formative.
Question and success checks
Which features of a way of working would fit what matters to me?

1. Compare at least three case patterns using shared headings and card evidence. 2. Link a feature to a preference and explain why it fits. 3. Name a trade-off or question before treating that fit as a firm choice.
Prepare

Books, pens, four case cards, vocabulary mat and usual reading or typing aids. Keep the adult key apart from first choices. No web, login or pupil phone. Use the cards as prepared sources, with labels beside claims.
Source adaptation

All four cases are invented and unnamed. A small bakery represents a small business; the hospital ward is part of the public sector in this example; a warehouse planning role represents a large employer; a repair worker runs their own business. The cases illustrate combinations of type, work status and pattern. They do not define every workplace. Generic settings replace real organisations and places. No actual vacancy, pay, contract right or entry rule is asserted.
Where this leads
This helps me compare work with what matters to me and ask useful questions before choosing a next step.
Forty minute teaching sequence
Phase
Min
Teaching and evidence
Retrieval
Recall how a source card can give a clue and still leave a gap. Neutral fallback: one example does not describe every job.
Explicit input
Separate employer type, employee/self-employed status and work pattern. Model a preference, case feature, reason and trade-off using A. Check that a label alone cannot prove fit.
Guided comparison

Read A–D. Compare fixed on-site work, on-site shifts, hybrid work and booked self-employed work. Discuss security, flexibility and support. Main hinge and parallel hinge; no one pattern is best for everyone.
Independent application
Choose at least three case patterns. Record comparable features and labels. Explain which feature fits a preference, why, and a trade-off or question. Give one next step and fade answer prompts.
Reflection
Ask the learner to justify a preferred pattern or type with evidence. Check all three comparisons. Retain first view, actual support and any change in the Careers Portfolio/action plan.
The five phases total 40 minutes. Reading, checks, feedback and access pauses sit within them. Slide 11 is an access reference; slide 12 is hidden for staff.
Worked example and fade

Practice model: “For this example, I value knowing my work days ahead. A has the same agreed weekdays, which could help me plan. Early starts may not fit me, so I would ask the exact times. B offers a rota, but the shifts change. C has agreed weekday hours, with a planned mix of office and remote work.” Point to A/B/C. A preference is a reason to investigate, not a final job decision.

Fade to a different feature: ask the learner to find support in B and C, then make their own comparison. They may include D. Retain normal reading or scribing access while answer prompts fade. Do not bank a copied model as personal preference evidence.
Check after explicit input

Ask privately: Does “small business” tell us the hours of every job there? Is hybrid work a mix of places or a promise to choose any hours? Expected: no; a mix of on-site and remote work. If unclear, point to the type and time/place fields and re-model the distinction.
Routes and planned access
Independent

Compare at least three of A–D using shared headings: time/place, flexibility, support and security or a question. Name type/status and pattern accurately. Link a chosen feature to a current preference with a reason, then a trade-off or next question. Cases are evidence for examples, not rules about every employer.
Supported

Use one card and one heading at a time. Begin with A/B/C; D remains available. Highlight labels, model one separate reason and use the vocabulary bank. Rehearse privately. Keep at least three patterns and a reason for fit as the target. Fade answer prompts where secure.
Floor

Use A/B/C and the printed choices with the cards visible. Read aloud or scribe the learner’s own choices. Compare three patterns, then ask which feature the learner values and why. Choosing three labels alone does not show comparison or personal fit. Record missing elements and any supplied answers as partial evidence.
Cognition and Learning

Use explicit instruction, a separate model and guided practice. Chunk by card and heading. Compare the same feature across cases. Repeat the feature–preference–reason routine, with extra processing time.
Communication and Interaction

Pre-teach employer, pattern, shift, hybrid, support and preference. Rehearse privately with short frames. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. Wait for thought; no cold calling or forced pair work.
SEMH

Keep a predictable sequence and private feedback. No household work, income or fixed future choice required. Offer a regulation break and planned return. A preference can be tentative and can change. A practice preference is available without pressure to disclose.
Sensory and Physical
Use clear print, a one-card view and normal aids. Do not infer what a learner can do from a case or their support needs. Discuss which support would help, without requiring health disclosure.
EAL
Plan in any language. Use examples to distinguish working place from working hours. Offer private oral rehearsal and a small word bank. Separate language access from comparative reasoning.

Record access separately from answer prompts. If a learner uses an invented preference, record hypothetical reasoning; the personal-fit part remains unconfirmed until the learner offers their own preference privately.
Staff prompts and checks
Hinge during guided comparison

C is hybrid work for a warehouse planning role. Which claim fits? A: Every warehouse worker can work remotely and choose any hours. B: This planning role mixes agreed places and keeps agreed hours. Answer B. Ask for the time/place lines. If insecure, separate job task, place and hours, re-model C, then use the parallel hinge.
Parallel hinge

D is self-employed and books work with customers. Which claim fits? A: The worker can always choose any hours and has guaranteed work. B: The worker can suggest times, but bookings and customers affect the plan. Answer B. Ask for a card clue. If insecure, compare D’s flexibility with its security line and retain a supported route.
Speaking frames

F: “Case ... works ... . The card says ... .” M: “A difference between ... and ... is ... . I value ... so ... could fit because ... .” H: “This feature may fit, but ... is a trade-off. I would check ... before choosing.”
TA focus

I do: check type, status, pattern and card label. We do: ask for a case clue, not a preferred answer. Independent: record access and actual answer prompts, then fade prompts where secure. Help with a calm return and a purposeful next question.
Prompt ladder
1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.
Misconceptions and corrections

“A large or public employer guarantees a secure job.” Type alone cannot establish the terms or length of a particular job. Check the contract and circumstances. “Flexible or self-employed means no limits on time.” Customers, agreed hours, tasks and support arrangements can constrain choices. No pattern is best for everyone.
Evidence and source end check

J12: Employer/work-pattern comparison. M12: Can the student justify one preferred working pattern or employer type? Check the reason and case feature. Also check the full outcome: at least three ways compared and features linked to preferences. One justified choice alone is not the whole outcome.
Assessment and safe teaching
What this lesson can evidence

Week 4 is formative. Keep a comparison of at least three patterns, source labels and relevant similarities/differences across common headings. Retain a preference, the linked feature and reason, plus a trade-off or question. Keep first thinking, actual support and any revision. The added trade-off/question supports cautious choice; assess the exact core outcome separately. A list of three names or a copied model is not enough.
Response and feedback

Book first. Type instead is an optional equivalent record. Reader, scribe, speech, pointing and typing are normal access. A learner may respond privately. If they choose a practice preference, log comparison and hypothetical reasoning without claiming their personal preference has been evidenced.

VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step. R requires Voice and Audience, NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult may be the audience. Use E only when actual evidence is banked.
Portfolio

Keep the comparison, preference type, reason, support and any revision in the Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work; no unit completion inferred. Use the open question as a next research step.
Teaching need next lesson ____________________ Next research question ____________________
Boundaries

Examples show possible arrangements only. Employer size/type, employee/self-employed status and work patterns can overlap in other combinations. The public-sector label applies only to this ward case; the hybrid pattern applies only to the warehouse planning role. Do not rank people or jobs by employer, pay or pattern. No household income, personal health or family employment disclosure. No legal or financial advice, actual employment terms or guaranteed outcomes. Follow the usual safeguarding route if needed.
Calendar and sequence

Year A. Autumn 2 Week 4, 23–27 November 2026. Tuesday 24 November, P3, 40 minutes. Week 6 retains mixed formative/summative source marking; Week 7 is assessing. Weeks 5–7 follow in order, one return after each Downloaded.

Staff answers and case guide
Scope of the examples
Invented teaching cases prepared 30 October 2026. These examples do not describe real jobs or rules for all workplaces.
Exact outcome: I can compare at least three ways of working and explain which features fit my preferences.

E12 includes small/medium businesses, public sector, large employers and self-employment. The cases distinguish employer type, work status and pattern. They are combinations, not four exclusive categories. A small or large employer could use other patterns; self-employed work could also be hybrid or on site.
Cases A and B
Field
A small bakery
B hospital ward
Type and status
Small business; employee.
Part of the public sector in this case; employee.
Pattern and place
Fixed early weekday shifts at the bakery.
Day/evening shifts and some weekends on the ward.
Flexibility
Changes need manager agreement. Fixed days may help planning.
Rota ahead; swaps need agreement and cover.
Support
Task demonstration/checks in a small team; limited people free at once.
Training and a lead on each shift; busy times affect help.
Security or gap
Agreed weekly hours; duration not stated. Ask exact times/contract terms.
Agreed hours; contract length not stated. Ask rota notice and cover.

Similarity: both sample roles work on site in teams (A/B). Difference: A’s times are the same agreed weekdays; B’s rota varies. Neither pattern is universally better. The ward case involves supplies only, with no clinical task or practical instruction.
Cases C and D and fit examples
Field
C warehouse planning role
D self employed repair worker
Type and status
Large employer; employee.
Own business; self-employed.
Pattern and place
Hybrid after training: two office days and three remote days each week.
Booked work at customer sites, with admin too.
Flexibility
Agreed weekdays/hours; planned place changes. No any-time promise.
Can suggest times; customers and tasks affect bookings.
Support
Check-ins and a contact. Kit, connection and workspace needed.
Arranges training and outside help; no employer-supplied lead in this case.
Security or gap
Agreed hours; length not stated. Ask kit provision and remote support.
Bookings, income and costs can vary. Ask about steady work and available help.
Examples of justified fit

Set days: A or C may fit, with A’s early starts or C’s remote-work needs as trade-offs. Team support: A, B or C may fit in different ways; the card does not promise instant help. More say over bookings: D may fit, with customer needs, admin and variable bookings as limits. Varied hours: B may fit a stated preference, but exact shifts and notice need checking.

Valid personal example: “I like set weekdays. A could fit because the days stay the same. I would check the early start time.” Valid practice reasoning uses the same structure but must be recorded as hypothetical. Preferences can change, and several options can fit.
Checks and misconceptions
Retrieval and model

Recall source label and limit from prior prepared-card research. Neutral fallback: one example does not describe every job. After the model: a small-business label does not determine all hours; hybrid refers to a mix of work places, not unlimited choice of time.
Main hinge

B is correct. C describes one planning role with agreed office/remote days and hours. It does not allow every warehouse worker to work remotely. Re-model job task, place and time if needed; then use the parallel hinge.
Parallel hinge

B is correct. D can suggest times, but customers and bookings constrain the plan. It does not promise constant work or full control. Ask for flexibility and security evidence; retain supported work if insecure.
Misconceptions

Employer size/type does not guarantee security. Particular terms and circumstances matter. Flexibility has dimensions: time, place or task may vary separately. Self-employment brings choices and responsibilities; it does not guarantee income or no constraints. A preference is not a permanent identity or a measure of someone’s worth.
Supported and Floor

Use one heading across A/B/C before moving on. Floor key A, A, B, A, B, A. Ask for card clues and an actual or practice preference with a reason. Labels alone are insufficient. Log answers supplied by an adult separately from reading or scribing access.
Safe discussion

Use the generic cases without real employer claims. No pressure to share household income, work history or health. Do not tell a learner that a pattern is unsuitable because of a diagnosis or support need. Ask which arrangements or support would help.
Evidence and feedback guide
Core evidence

J12 calls for employer/work-pattern comparison. The exact outcome requires at least three ways of working and explained fit to preferences. In this pack, collect three case patterns under common headings, labels beside claims, and a feature–preference–reason link. The trade-off or question is an added cautious-choice check; record it separately from the core outcome. M12 tests one justified preference, so also check breadth of comparison.
Secure and partial evidence

Secure: “A and B are on site; A keeps the same weekdays while B has changing shifts. C mixes office and remote days. I value knowing my days, so A could fit, but I need its start time.” Check support and security discussion too. Partial: three names without features; only two patterns; a preference with no reason; or a copied model. Hypothetical fit alone does not establish the learner’s personal preference.
Precise next steps

“Add a third way of working.” “Compare the same feature in both cases.” “Link the case feature to what you value.” “Name the detail you need to check.” Give one next step and keep the learner’s response.
Access and independence

Normal reader, scribe, typing or aids do not by themselves reduce independence of thought. Record actual answer prompts separately and fade them where secure. Keep a private response route. If the learner chooses a practice preference, bank the comparison and offer a later private opportunity for the personal-fit element.
Portfolio and marking

Retain comparison, case labels, preference type, reason, support and revision in the Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. VF verbal feedback; WS supported; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read back; E actual banked evidence; R after Voice, Audience, NS and response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode.
Fidelity boundary

Exact G12 outcome, I12 sequence and K12 routes retained. Generic invented cases meet the owner’s unnamed-employer requirement. No real employment terms are verified. Week 4 formative; Week 6 mixed source marking; Week 7 assessing.
Cases A and B
Invented teaching cases prepared 30 October 2026. These examples do not describe real jobs or rules for all workplaces.
Case A Small bakery
Type or status: Small business. Employee. Pattern: Fixed hours on site.
The worker helps prepare and pack bread in a small team. Work is at the bakery. The agreed shifts start early on the same weekdays.
Flexibility: A change of shift needs agreement with the manager. Fixed hours help with planning, but an early start may not suit everyone.
Support: A team member shows the tasks and checks work. In a small team, fewer people may be free to help at once.
Security: Weekly hours are agreed in this example. The card does not say how long the job lasts.
Question: What are the exact start times and the contract terms?
Case B Hospital ward
Type or status: Public sector in this example. Employee. Pattern: Shifts on site.
The worker checks and puts away ward supplies with the team. No care task is part of this example. Work is on the ward. A rota includes different day and evening shifts, and some weekends.
Flexibility: The rota is shared ahead of time. A shift swap needs agreement so the team has cover.
Support: The worker has task training and a lead to ask on each shift. Busy times may affect when help is available.
Security: Hours are agreed, but contract length is not stated. A public sector label alone does not prove a job is secure.
Question: How far ahead is the rota shared, and what cover is available?
Cases C and D
Invented teaching cases prepared 30 October 2026. These examples do not describe real jobs or rules for all workplaces.
Case C Warehouse planning role
Type or status: Large employer. Employee. Pattern: Hybrid weekday work.

The worker plans orders and keeps records for a warehouse. Moving goods still happens on site. This planning role has two days in the warehouse office and three at an agreed remote workspace each week, after training.
Flexibility: Weekday hours are agreed. The work location varies on planned days; it is not a choice to work at any time.
Support: The team has check-ins and a contact for help. Remote work needs suitable kit, a connection and a space to work.
Security: Weekly hours are agreed. Contract length is not stated. A large employer does not guarantee a lasting job.
Question: Who provides the kit, and how can I get help on a remote day?
Case D Self employed repair worker
Type or status: Own small business. Self-employed. Pattern: Work booked with customers.
The worker books simple repair tasks, does the agreed work and keeps job records. Work takes place at customer sites. Times are agreed for each booking.
Flexibility: The worker can suggest times, but customers and the work also affect the plan. Admin takes time too.
Support: The worker arranges training and can seek help from other skilled workers. There is no team lead supplied by an employer in this case.
Security: Bookings can change, so work and income can vary. Costs and time between jobs matter. No amount of future work is promised.
Question: How steady are bookings, and what help can I arrange?
A model and your comparison
A practice reason
For this example, I value knowing my work days ahead. A has the same agreed weekdays. This could help me plan. An early start may not suit me, so I would ask the exact times.
B has a rota with changing shifts. C has agreed weekday hours and a planned mix of work places. D agrees times for each booking. These features may fit different needs.
Your task in your book
Choose at least three cases from A–D. Use the same headings: time and place; flexibility; support; security or a question. Keep the card label beside each point.
Name a preference, a feature that may fit and why. Add a trade-off or a question you would check. You do not need to make a final career choice.
Preference ideas
I may value set days, varied times, team help, a mix of work places, or more say in bookings. No one feature is best for everyone. More than one case could fit.
You can give your own reason to an adult in private. You may use a practice preference instead. Staff record which kind you used.
Read, point, speak, write, type or use a scribe. Plan in any language. Keep your first view and any change.
Floor choices and short frames
Use A, B and C with the cards in view. An adult may read and record your own choices.
Check
Choices
Three patterns
A: A fixed on site; B shifts on site; C hybrid. B: All three have the same pattern.
A and B
A: Both work at the workplace, but their times differ. B: Both work remotely.
C hybrid work
A: Anyone can choose any hours. B: This role mixes agreed places and keeps agreed hours.
Support
A: The cards describe different kinds of team help. B: Every worker always gets instant help.
Security
A: A type label proves a job will last. B: Check the terms and what is still unknown.
A practice preference for set days
A: A may fit, but check its early starts. B: A is best for everyone.
My reason
“I value ... . Case ... has ... . This could fit because ... .”
“A trade-off is ... . Before choosing, I would ask ... .”
Use the same headings for three cases in your book or with a scribe. A practice choice is not proof of your own preference. You may answer privately.
Adult key for the choices
Keep this page apart from first choices. Record the learner’s answers before giving the key.
Check
Answer and reason
Three patterns
A: Fixed on site, shifts on site and hybrid differ.
A and B
A: Both on site, with different time patterns.
Hybrid
B: C mixes agreed places while keeping agreed hours.
Support
A: Small-team help, shift-team help and remote check-ins differ.
Security
B: The job terms and missing detail matter.
Practice fit
A: Set days may fit; early starts remain a trade-off.

Floor key A, A, B, A, B, A. Ask the learner to point to the card clue. The choices alone do not show the full comparison or a personal preference. Keep any missing fields or supplied answers as partial evidence.

There is no single correct preferred case. A valid reason links a real case feature to the preference used. If a practice preference is used, log hypothetical reasoning; offer a private way to confirm personal fit without pressure.
Words for ways of working
Word
Meaning
employer
A person or group that employs workers.
small business
A business with a small team in our example.
SME
A small or medium-sized business.
public sector
Work run by public bodies for the public.
work pattern
How work time or place is arranged.
on site
At the workplace.
shift
A set period of work on a rota.
hybrid
A mix of work on site and at a remote place.
self-employed
Running your own work or business.
flexibility
Room to change an arrangement, within its limits.
security
How steady or lasting work may be. Check the terms.
preference
Something you would like or value.
trade-off
A gain may come with a drawback.
Words for my reason
I value ... . This feature could fit because ... . A trade-off is ... . I would check ... .
Plan in any language. You may read, point, speak, type or use your normal aid.
